Messages.Author: Andrew 'Wes' Weston
Messages.Body:
I think that, with the original base game, contesting vampires could
sometimes be a good thing for the game as it forced people to stop playing
Malkavian S&B over and over and over again, for fear of your predator and
prey doing the same (which was often the case, at least in my old playgroup
*sigh*). In other words, it forced us to be creative... to diversify. It was
a pain when it happened, but it was also pretty easy to avoid: just don't
play with Gilbert Duane.

After seeing a few disastrous game situations lately, though, I would like
to once again make the case that we should change the rules for contesting
vampires.

When the rules for contesting were first developed in the original Jyhad
set, there were a total of 111 vampires. Now, there are 1061 vampires. The
chance of contesting a vampire is much, much lower than it was before,
granted, but when it occurs it is just as game-destroying, if not more so,
than it ever was.

There are many creative and interesting decks that are centred around
individual vampires. A deck built around one particular vampire is
completely destroyed if that vampire is contested. Chances are that both
methuselahs are building around that vampire for some reason, and chances
are that the vampire is not a weenie, so now you have two decks essentially
shut down because neither player can play it as it was intended. Is this
fair to those players? Is it a good thing to give the *other* Methuselahs a
distinct advantage and/or an unbalanced table? To me, it seems contrary to
the Predator-Prey relationship much of the time, unless one is playing with
Betrayer maybe.

Even thematically, contesting is flawed, in my opinion. Think about what is
happening when two powerful vampires are vying for control over a lesser
vampire. Why would that vampire become paralyzed? That vampire would
probably feel the effect of being tugged in two different directions,
certainly, but they would still be able to perform tasks. They'd probably be
very unlikely to take actions against one of the Methuselahs controlling
them however.

Let's say that Frederick the Weak is being contested by Methuselah A and
Methuselah B. Here are some ideas for how this could be handled less
disruptively:

1) On Methuselah A's turn, Frederick is turned right side up, becoming
controlled and untapped. Methuselah B's copy of Frederick is turned upside
down, becoming uncontrolled until their coming turn.

Rationale: Only one version of Frederick should be active at any given time.
Note that one Methuselah will control Frederick for more game time than the
other, depending on where they are seated, adding some interesting tactical
considerations.

2) On Methuselah A's turn, Methuselah A's Frederick can take no (D) actions
against Methuselah B or anything that B controls.

Rationale: Frederick would be unlikely to take actions against either of his
masters.

3) If Frederick burns, then he is burned for both Methuselahs (unless he
becomes uncontested, ie due to an oust). Similarly, if Frederick goes to
torpor, both copies of Frederick go to torpor.

Rationale: An incentive to cooperate or abuse depending on the relationship
between the two contesting Methuselahs.

These are just suggestions... there are probably easier ways to do it.

The advantages to these changes should be obvious. With those two
Methuselahs able to play their decks as they intended, the game becomes more
interesting and less unbalanced. Nobody gets a free ride to victory because
their predator or prey is tied down with a contested vampire. A player can
actually have fun for a two hour game instead of wishing it was over.

(Note that I have not touched on contesting of unique locations, allies,
titles, etc. I don't think those rules are quite as disruptive and generally
work well as is.)

Thoughts?

Cheers,
WES

While I like the idea of vampires being able to act while contested, I
think that may cause unforeseen problems when they are both active.

What if the contestation rule were amended like this:

"The cost to contest a card is one pool, which *any Methuselah may* pay
during each of your untap phases. Instead of paying the cost to contest
the card, you may choose to yield the card. A yielded card is burned."

So you can briefly appeal to other Meths to assist you in contesting
vampires or other resources. This way if two "star" decks contest, that
gives the other 2-3 Meths at the table some incentive to keep things
balanced, though they don't have to help if they don't want. The Meth
controlling the contested card should have the option to refuse help
and let the contested card burn of course.

I agree, but for the sake of discussion, here's a fantastical rules
change (in BOLD):

****************

4.1. Contested Cards

Some of the cards in the game represent unique resources, such as
specific locations, equipment or people. These cards will be identified
as "unique" in their card text. In addition, all vampire cards
represent unique vampires.

If more than one copy of a unique LIBRARY card is brought into play,
that means control of the card is being contested. For the duration of
the contest, all copies of the contested card are turned face down and
are out of play. If an additional copy of an already-contested card is
brought into play, it is immediately contested and turned face down as
well.

The cost to contest a LIBRARY card is one pool, which you pay during

each of your untap phases. Instead of paying the cost to contest the

card, you may choose to yield the card. A yielded card is burned. Any
cards or counters stacked on the yielded card are also burned.

IF A CRYPT CARD IS CONTESTED, ALL COPIES OF THE CONTESTED CARD ARE
TURNED FACE DOWN AND ARE OUT OF PLAY. DURING YOUR UNTAP PHASE, YOU MUST
BURN AT LEAST ONE POOL TO CONTINUE CONTESTING THE CARD. IF MORE THAN
ONE POOL WAS BURNED TO CONTEST THE CARD SINCE YOUR LAST TURN, YOU MUST
BURN AT LEAST THAT AMOUNT. YOU MAY ALSO CHOOSE TO YIELD THE CARD
INSTEAD OF PAYING THE COST.

EXAMPLE: BETH CONTROLS FREDERICK THE WEAK. ON JOSH'S TURN, HE
INFLUENCES INTO PLAY A SECOND COPY OF FREDERICK, AND BOTH COPIES ARE
TURNED FACE TO DENOTE THE CONTEST. ON BETH'S TURN, SHE BURNS ONE POOL
TO CONTINUE CONTESTING FREDERICK WITH JOSH. ON JOSH'S NEXT TURN, HE
BURNS ONE POOL, AND DECIDES TO BURN THREE MORE POOL. ON BETH'S NEXT
TURN, SHE MUST DECIDE WHETHER OR NOT TO YIELD, BURN FOUR POOL TO
CONTINUE THE CONTEST (THE AMOUNT JOSH BURNED ON HIS LAST TURN), OR BURN
FIVE OR MORE POOL TO ENCOURAGE JOSH TO YIELD ON HIS NEXT TURN.

If all other copies of a card you are contesting are yielded, then the
card is untapped and turned face up during your next untap phase,
ending the contest.

Be careful about putting duplicates of the same unique cards in your
deck. You can't control more than one of the same unique card at a
time, and you cannot contest cards with yourself (if some effect would
force you to contest a card with yourself, then you simply burn the
incoming copy of the unique card). On the other hand, you may wish to
have a second copy handy in case the first is burned.

**********************

Something like the above would certainly shorten contests, I think,
when contesters are sitting next to each other, anyway.

Sorry, I think you're mis-reading what I meant by rock/paper/scissors.
It is, of course, sometimes used to refer to the classic triumvirate of
bleed/vote/rush. But...

>any
> more than the existing archetypes like walls, powerbleed and such. Most
> star vampire decks I've seen are either combat or one-trick-pony decks,

...one trick pony decks are a sort of rock/paper/scissors. That is, if
your deck goes off, it can work fabulously. But if it doesn't, it can
be hell.

Now, some one-trick pony decks can also be intelligently put together -
much like a star-vampire deck with useful back-up. For example, a 45
Cryptic Mission deck can have useful backup with, say, Theft of Vitae
and Computer Hacking and some decent hand cycling, so when you find
yourself up against Imbued or a deck that can generate blood at
inconvenient times annoyingly, you can fall back onto other options.

Bad one trick ponies will find themselves up against their nemeses and
just collapse. Which is bad for that table - the predator/prey dynamic
is all out of kilter from turn one - and bad for V:TES more generally if
that situation replicates itself.

Analogously, this is why I also think that things like the weenie
pot/cel decks that Peter Bakija has put together over many years can
benefit so much from Computer Hacking. (Moving from a classic archetype
of 12 Rushes, 4 Havens towards something like 8 Rushes, 6-8 Computer
Hackings and 4 Havens.) Strength through diversity, but without hugely
harming the deck.

The bigger problem is that a number of such decks can be extremely
intricate and potentially powerful *if* they go off. But a complete
nightmare if they don't. Encouraging situations where they don't go off
being mitigated can encourage even stupider decks, IME, which also
brings its own problems.

My experience is that I don't like seeing *bad* one-trick ponies and
*bad* star-vampire decks, and that mitigating problems like "What
happens when we both bring Arika out?" will encourage more of the bad
sort of deck that doesn't have strength outside that situation. Because
if you don't have strength in the rest of the deck *somehow*, losing the
key vampire is still going to screw you - just not through contesting.

Whatever the term for that sort of setup is, that's what I meant. Which
is what I was meaning by "all or bust", pretty much.

> The advantages to these changes should be obvious. With those two

IMHO, your starting point (avoiding unbalancing of the table) is very
good, since nobody should gain such advantage as contesting Arika
between his predator and his prey.
But I don't like your solution. The vampire must be unique around the
table. To my mind, the main root of the problem is time. Should one
Methuselah be forced to yield immediately, it would be better - still
unbalancing, though. But this can be balanced at least relatively. What
about such rules:

When a player brings into play a second copy of a unique vampire, this
immediately starts the contest. That player can offer some pool to gain
control of the vampire, and all players contesting the same vampire can
make bids. Whoever wins the bidding, pays the stated amount of pool and
gains control of the vampire. All other players keep their pool, spent
on the vampire, back.

Why do I think this is better? Because there is no stalling, and nobody
loses too much. The contest is solved immediately, and both players can
continue playing. One get a vampire, another gets his pool back, so no
one takes too heavy penalty. Notice that even if you lose a contest,
you still can generate pool, influence ANOTHER copy of the vampire and
contest him once again!

I even think that the same rule can be applied to all unique cards, not
just vampires. What if I could pay extra pool for the Dreams, if I
would really want to get it and to take it from another player, without
waiting for 3 turns?

It would be great to know people's opinion about this suggestion.

Yours,
Ector

Bzzzt.

Intelligent back-up can be there for all sorts of reasons. Like
whatever it is your star vampire does turning out to be a complete crock
because you happened to be sat next to a deck that just doesn't care
about that. Are you playing a multi-acting star-vampire Baltimore Purge
deck, that untaps to get Renewed Vigor, then Graverob a vampire, then
Baltimore Purge, with a few Mind Rapes and some blood gain in there for
good measure? Okay. Now you want intelligent back-up. Where does that
deck not work at all? Against a heavy ally deck, for a start, but most
particularly the Imbued. What happens when you sit next to the Imbued
without any other options? Your deck collapses in a heap, and you have
nothing else to do.

So, you include intelligent backup for other situations. This situation
can be for when your strategy doesn't work because the Imbued sat down
next to you, but it can also be for other situations, like when the star
vampire you've chosen to do it gets eaten/stolen/beaten/Banished or
whatever. You have a backup plan to get out of jail. If you've
constructed a good deck, it's an intelligent backup plan at that.

You can, of course, also include those other options in your main
strategy. For example, your weenie vampires might be there to bleed
your prey when all else fails, but they might also be there to fuel some
other aspect of your deck - such as an Al-MonkeyTim deck going along
with a whole bunch of Caitiff. If the main strategy of the deck works,
it can feed the Caitiff to Mr MonkeyTim. If the main strategy of the
deck fails, it can fall back on weenie bleed.

Various similar strategies abound. Many of them turn into weenie-
something, but that's sort of inevitable when most (but not all) star
vampire decks focus around a big vampire, so you want your other
vampires to be cheap, for simple reasons of pool cost. The most obvious
exception I can think of would be The Eldest are Tsunda, where Tsunda is
cheap anyway and so you can have some weenie Ravnos and some midcaps.

Your weenie bleed could also be weenie pool gain bitches, in the right
deck. If you happen to have the right vampire (e.g. Anson) or throw in
some library resources, you can fuel a bunch of hunting and Blood Dolls.
Or hunting and Heidelberg. (Or a bit of both!) And, of course, they
can weenie bleed. Depending on your deck construction choice and the
vampires you have to hand, they might even be able to bleed at stealth -
say, a super-star vampire who pulls off the occasional Psychic Veil.

It can, as alluded to earlier, also be there for when your star vampire
gets mushed, as much as your strategy getting whipped out from under
you. Need a rescue? Intelligent backup. Got whipped by a Pentex
Subversion? Intelligent backup. Even though you can, of course, take
steps to negate or reduce the impact of such strategies, it's rare for
them to be entirely successful. Even with a whole bunch of Wash in your
deck, you won't always pull one. You'll find yourself on the end of an
unblockable Mind Rape at some point. Whatever.

Whatever it is, if your star vampire goes tits up, intelligent backup is
the way forward.

>As for whether it's a problem, of course it is. Since
>people seem to like building decks that are entirely based on a single
>vampire, that by itself is a reason to permit them. I see no reason why
>any drawback is particularly necessary for reasons of game balance, and
>certainly not one which is so chaotic in its effect.

If we assume that star decks without intelligent backup that get creamed
by someone trumping them *somehow* lead to unhelpful tables, it's a pain
in the ass. I play my bad deck that gets ass-raped because you played
the nemesis and I had nothing else to do. But that causes problems for
the *rest* of the table. It's not just my deck. It's not just my
decision.

When you're in a two-player game, like Magic, poor play generates its
own rewards. Occasionally, of course, it'll get lucky - a good shuffle,
an ill-thought-out experiment that turns out to be worthwhile, a deck
that doesn't think about new facets of the game X, Y and Z (whatever
they might be) but it works out fine because that deck never sees a deck
exploiting those facets. But overall, on average, a poor deck will get
knocked out in early rounds, and the player will need to improve to
progress further. The better player will simply find themself with an
easier round.

We sit down at a table, I'm bleeding you. My deck dies in a heap,
because you are playing the anti-deck. Okay. So you get a free game,
so your prey isn't happy. I can't do anything at all, so my predator
has this inactive lump between him and his next prey, which skews his
whole game all randomly. That's three players who are being randomly
affected by my deck crashing and burning.

Now, if we move to a situation where players playing star-vampire decks
are *actively encouraged* to put in many, many more copies of their star
vampire, to encourage them to have two, three, four in their
uncontrolled region - in order to burn those vampires to force an end to
the contest - players don't have those other options. They don't have
the weenies to rescue the star. They don't have extra vampires to burn
an annoying card, such as a Smiling Jack or a Madness Network. They're
actively encouraged to play All Star All The Time, which means that the
dynamic of tables is screwed whenever they find that their deck is
screwed by something, be it contestation, a well-timed Banishment or
Sensory Deprivation, massive combat, the anti-strategy being sat next to
it, Pentex Subversion, or whatever.

I don't see that that helps the game.

>The main reason to
>have the existing drawback is completely for thematic and historical
>reasons. It can also be excused in that it's a very rare occurance and
>gets rarer all the time with each new expansions worth of vampires.

That that's why it was created in the first place, yes.

However, actively encouraging players to fill their decks with one
vampire causes a potential crap-load of other problems, in the round. I
put your star-vampire into torpor and keep it there, you can't influence
a second copy out to fix that. If your deck isn't intelligently
constructed to deal with this situation, bye bye.

Sure. I understand this point and I agree with it. Unfortunately, what
you're talking about is a problem not just to star vampire decks but to
any focused, single-strategy deck. Terming them "bad decks" is beside
the point, as far as I can see. If the players view the potential payoff
to the gamble of focusing a deck on its one trick as being higher than
the drawback when their opponents have the perfect foil for that trick (or
when a star vampire isn't available to be influenced out for whatever
reason), then the deck will get built. If the perception is accurate, the
deck isn't bad - it's just risky. It actually might be a rather good deck
on the whole.

The fact of the matter is that the rule covering uniqueness in vampires
doesn't really have a discernable role in discouraging dependence on a
particular vampire. It's possible that rule was intended for that purpose
in the case of certain library cards, but if it was ever the intended
purpose for vampires, it's basically become irrelevant by now. Now, I
think it's fair to look at it as just a completely random screw that takes
place on very rare occasions that does all the terrible things to table
balance you describe above when it takes place (setting aside the possibility
of a Betrayer deck, of course). I personally don't think it's a common
enough occurrence to warrant any of the solutions I've seen proposed, but
I can't blame people for proposing them. Trying to frame proposals like
this as being counter-productive just because you want to portray star
vampire decks as being "bad" because (in turn), you've focused only on the
drawbacks of using a star vampire and not its advantages is just wrong.

> Now, if we move to a situation where players playing star-vampire decks
> are *actively encouraged* to put in many, many more copies of their star
> vampire, to encourage them to have two, three, four in their
> uncontrolled region - in order to burn those vampires to force an end to
> the contest - players don't have those other options.

difference in people's deckbuilding. You're talking about an incentive to
alter a crypt makeup to cover an extremely rare situation so I think your
fear of that particular proposal making the situation discernibly worse is
completely unfounded. What it does is just give one of the two decks a
potential 'out' so that at least one of them can get back in the ball game.
I don't think it really solves the problem since the loser is still
screwed (and unbalances the table, yadda, yadda) and the winner was probably
going to sustain high damage to his position due to the delay and extra cost
to winning the contest but the end result is likely to be a better game, even
so. I just think the whole thing is not really worth the complexity of
adding it to the rules for such an unlikely, if terrible, situation.
Especially given that it doesn't completely fix the problem.

> I don't see that that helps the game.

It would. It just wouldn't help all that much.

Fred
